Anxiety, treated with cognitive behavioural therapy in her fifties
family_history: Mother had Alzheimer's disease diagnosed at 72
Father died of myocardial infarction at 66

social_history.driving: Driving, with difficulty reading road signs on the left reported by her husband

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. MoCA 22/30. The pattern is unusual: she loses points on the cube, the clock, serial sevens and delayed recall, but on focused testing she cannot name her own fingers on either hand, cannot distinguish right from left reliably, cannot perform written calculation beyond single digits, and writes with letter omissions and reversals. Naming of objects is intact; reading aloud is intact for words but she loses her place in a line of text.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Visual fields full to confrontation on repeated testing. Face symmetric. Speech fluent without paraphasia.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk, tone and strength. No drift, no tremor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to primary modalities. Graphaesthesia impaired in the right hand.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact. Ideomotor praxis intact to command.
neurological_exam.additional: Finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia and dyscalculia together — the four elements of Gerstmann's syndrome. Pulse regular at 68.

patient.chief_complaint: Six months of difficulty with writing, calculating and organising, which she and her family fear is early Alzheimer's disease
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Silvia Donati is a 64-year-old primary school teacher who attends with her husband, convinced she has early Alzheimer's disease because her mother was diagnosed at 72. Six months ago, over a single afternoon, she found she could not write the class register or add up marks; the episode lasted several hours and her general practitioner attributed it to stress. She returned to work but has not been able to teach since: she cannot mark arithmetic, mixes up left and right when directing children, and makes letter errors when writing on the board. She has been on sick leave for four months. Her husband adds that she loses her place when reading and has twice missed a turning on the left while driving. Her memory for events and conversations is, in his account, essentially normal — she runs the household diary and has not missed an appointment. The change was abrupt and dates to that afternoon; there has been no progression over six months. She has hypertension treated for eight years and takes a statin. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment. She is anxious about the diagnosis and asks directly whether she has her mother's disease.

findings.location: Focal at the infarct; medial temporal lobes normal

volumetrics.lesion_volume: 2.4 mL in the left angular gyrus

additional_observations: The infarct is centred on the left angular gyrus, the lesion site classically associated with Gerstmann's syndrome
No restricted diffusion — the infarct is chronic and dates to the episode six months ago
Hippocampi are normal with no medial temporal atrophy, which argues against Alzheimer's disease in a 64-year-old with cognitive complaints
SWI shows no microbleeds; Fazekas 1 white matter change only
mri.impression: Chronic infarct of the left angular gyrus with a minimal small-vessel burden and no medial temporal atrophy. The lesion location accounts precisely for the Gerstmann tetrad and dates to the episode misattributed to stress six months ago.

labs.interpretation: LDL 134 mg/dL is above target for a patient with a documented cerebral infarct. TSH, B12, folate, RPR and HIV are normal or negative, excluding reversible causes of a focal cognitive syndrome.

advanced_imaging.tracer_or_protocol: Time-of-flight and contrast-enhanced MR angiography of the head and neck

findings.signal: Patent M1, M2 and angular branches, no stenosis
No stenosis, no dissection, no fibromuscular change

advanced_imaging.impression: Normal angiography of the head and neck. No large-artery source, no dissection and no vasculitic appearance. The infarct is attributable to distal branch occlusion, and secondary prevention is medical.

quantitative_data.memory: within normal limits on free recall and recognition

specialized_test.impression: A circumscribed left parietal syndrome: finger localisation, right-left orientation, written calculation and writing are all at or below the 3rd percentile while verbal memory, naming and fluency are entirely within normal limits. This is not the profile of early Alzheimer's disease, in which delayed recall is the first and most affected domain.

scores.writing_sample: letter omissions and reversals without paraphasia

findings.performance: Finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia, dyscalculia — the Gerstmann tetrad, severely impaired
3/5 unaided, 5/5 cued; day-to-day memory intact by informant report — relatively spared
Serial sevens impaired, partly through the dyscalculia
Fluent, naming intact, no paraphasia — spared
Cube and clock impaired; loses place in a line of text

clinical_assessment.impression: MoCA 22/30 conceals a focal syndrome: finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia and dyscalculia together constitute Gerstmann's syndrome and localise to the left angular gyrus. Episodic memory is relatively preserved and cue-responsive, which is the opposite of the expected profile in Alzheimer's disease. Onset was abrupt and there has been no progression in six months.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.query: vascular cognitive impairment diagnostic criteria and secondary prevention

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — strategic single-infarct type, left angular gyrus infarct producing Gerstmann's syndrome with loss of occupational function

differential.key_features: The family history and the patient's own conviction make this the presumptive diagnosis on referral, but memory is normal on formal testing, the hippocampi show no atrophy, the onset was abrupt over one afternoon and there has been no progression in six months
A parietal presentation in a younger patient, but it is insidious and progressive with bilateral parieto-occipital atrophy, none of which is present here

differential.diagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack with functional overlay
differential.key_features: The deficits are objectively present six months later and anatomically coherent with a demonstrated infarct
The initial attribution to stress; but finger agnosia and right-left disorientation are not produced by anxiety, and the infarct is visible
Naming, fluency and repetition are intact and the syndrome is parietal rather than linguistic

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Abrupt onset over one afternoon six months ago with no progression since, a focal parietal syndrome rather than an amnestic one, and preserved day-to-day memory corroborated by the informant

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 22/30 concealing the complete Gerstmann tetrad — finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia, dyscalculia — with relatively preserved episodic memory, localising to the left angular gyrus

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; LDL 134 mg/dL above target for a patient with a documented infarct

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Chronic left angular gyrus infarct with Fazekas 1 change and no medial temporal atrophy — a strategic cortical lesion explaining the Gerstmann tetrad

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Isolated left parietal syndrome with preserved memory storage — a focal profile incompatible with early Alzheimer's disease

optimal_actions.action: Obtain MR angiography of the head and neck for intracranial large-artery stenosis or dissection
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No large-artery stenosis, occlusion or dissection; the infarct is embolic or small-vessel in origin and no proximal lesion requires treatment

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Institute secondary prevention after a documented infarct — blood pressure toward a systolic below 130 mmHg, high-intensity statin to an LDL below 70 mg/dL, single antiplatelet therapy — refer for cognitive rehabilitation targeting the parietal deficits, arrange an occupational assessment of fitness to teach with a formal driving assessment, and address her explicit fear of Alzheimer's disease with the biomarker-free evidence available
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Secondary prevention started, rehabilitation and occupational assessment arranged, and the Alzheimer question answered on the basis of the profile and the imaging rather than left unaddressed

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Test parietal functions specifically — finger naming, right-left orientation, written calculation, writing — because the screen does not capture them
Recognise that abrupt onset with no progression over six months is a stroke syndrome, not a degenerative one
Obtain brain MRI: the lesion location explains the syndrome and dates the event
Document normal memory on formal testing, which is what excludes early Alzheimer's disease here
Institute secondary prevention after a documented infarct
Address fitness to work and to drive, and answer the family's question about Alzheimer's disease explicitly
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose early Alzheimer's disease from a family history and a cognitive complaint when memory testing is normal and onset was abrupt
Do not attribute an abrupt focal cognitive syndrome to stress or anxiety
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor for a strategic infarct syndrome
Do not clear her to return to teaching or to drive without formal assessment of the parietal deficits
key_reasoning_points: The Gerstmann tetrad localises: finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia and dyscalculia together point to the left angular gyrus, and a lesion there was found
In early Alzheimer's disease delayed recall is the first domain to fail; normal free recall and recognition with a severe parietal syndrome is the wrong shape for it
Abrupt onset in one afternoon with six months of stability is the temporal signature of an infarct, and the family history is the reason the temporal signature was ignored
A cognitive syndrome can cost a patient her occupation without touching her memory, and the assessment must therefore be functional as well as diagnostic
The absence of medial temporal atrophy in a 64-year-old with cognitive complaints is a strong negative for Alzheimer's disease and can be obtained from the same MRI that shows the infarct

red_herrings.data_point: A mother with Alzheimer's disease diagnosed at 72
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the entire assessment on early Alzheimer's disease, which is also what the patient believes she has
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Late-onset Alzheimer's disease in one parent confers modest risk; here memory is normal, the hippocampi show no atrophy, onset was abrupt and the deficit is a focal parietal syndrome with a visible lesion

red_herrings.data_point: Longstanding anxiety and a general practitioner's attribution to stress
red_herrings.intended_effect: Supports a functional explanation for the initial episode and delays imaging
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Finger agnosia and right-left disorientation are not produced by anxiety, they persist six months later, and the angular gyrus infarct is visible on MRI

key_educational_points: Gerstmann's syndrome localises to the left angular gyrus and can be missed entirely by a screening instrument
Normal delayed recall on formal testing is a powerful argument against early Alzheimer's disease
Abrupt onset followed by stability is the temporal signature of a vascular lesion
A focal cognitive syndrome can destroy occupational function while sparing memory
